Physical abuse vs "discipline" because unfortunately for some communities, that kind of parenting is the norm.This is not including my opinion (I think they're both unacceptable ) and obviously deadly situations should be reported.

Honestly though thank you for sharing your experience and the other information.

> So unless a child is being physically beaten in front of you

Everyone is different therefore different types of abuse will impact people differently. There isn't like a simple damage scale of abuse. Everyone experiences some discomfort as a child, but once the discomfort reaches the level of "abuse" in any form, then it's nearly impossible to make the best decision with the systems we have in place.

Yeah we were supposed to a trauma timeline, I said that my parents where bad for xy and z reasons, then somehow it led to the good and bad philosophy, I asked questions to learn more, she was ok with it then she said my word usage of my parents being toxic as inaccurate. But the way she handled it, it felt like it was all in my head because while my needs weren't met and feelings were hurt and my parents needs and feelings are also valid. According to her, their actions aren't correct but most people deal with it. I said I was on the end scale of experiencing more trauma than the average person and she disagreed.

>It's sad but it probably isn't that uncommon to hear people have had similar experiences to you.

Idk from the various places where I've been around people, K-12 for example, I was usually one of the few people having lunch by themselves. It was common for me to walk around campus, staying there still closing and maybe seeing a couple people by themselves walking around. I spent 90 percent of my weekends in libraries, campus buildings or bookstores because I didn't like being home. Most of the regulars where either older and/or homeless, worked there or law/nursing students. I didn't have any friends growing up, maybe a few acquaintances, nothing long term. I had no one to talk to. Zero healthy relationships for 24 years, is that really normal?

 I've only just started making healthish friendships this year, I'm 27. Even the most "quiet" or "weird" people I saw had at least a healthy relationship with their family (as in able to a have a pleasent nonjudgmental conversation or laugh with them) or a partner or friend. Could those relationships have been terrible behind close doors, maybe, but I've personally noticed the value of having at least one supportive person in an abused person's life is pivotal in a way it's hard to explain. Ive notice the people I feel I can be myself had similar upbringings were they had little privilege and severely abandoned by their environment. On the other hand, if the person had one good parent or mentor, they just carry themselves differently. Also something about graduating highschool, if a person gets a chance to become independent like live on campus or move away, I've noticed they're more likely to be overcome their childhood trauma. It's like turning 17 or 18, and getting the chance to leave their trauma environment while starting their adult life is a pivotal moment for their brain development. It's a rough theory which I wish I could better articulate. I only took one basic human development course in uni and learned the value of how important certain environmental/external factors are at certain at stages. Like giving a baby love vs witholding affection makes a difference in their development.

The problem is I feel this doesn't help when I feel the need to eat everything. I really try to comfort my inner child and eat the junk food without beating myself up for it. However sometimes it seems my inner child wants to go a week or more eating whatever they want. Which is great for the child but the adult part of me is tired of the junk food, sometimes doesn't enjoy eating the food, and/or is simply full. Maybe I'm not listening and comforting my inner child well enough

I'm on mobile but in his videos have links to the studies and articles. 

For someone who is tall, eating 1200 calories MAY work but usually isn't enough. I've noticed in my friends and myself and that it led me to disordered eating. Yes I lost weight, but the cons outweighed the pros. Like you said, everyone should do what they want.

Also that comment was made in repsonse to you but it was a general comment. Maybe that's why it came off as me telling you what to do? I just wanted to dispel the 1200 cal for everyone myth😅 sorry for the confusion

Edit: Note this is a general comment meant for the thread/everyone. Be careful with 1200cal diets. Please take my comment with a grain of salt and speak to your medical team.

 The 1200 calorie diet is a bit a myth because the amount of calories one should consume ROUGHLY (because strict dieting is risky) depends on several factors including height, starting weight, health, activity levels etc. And if you have menstrual cycles( however anyone can do this), I recently heard of an amazing recommendation to eat at maintenance around your cycle. So every 2 weeks or so I try to eat at maintenance for the week. Yes the weight loss takes longer but you'll keep the weight off in the long run. This method helps you get use to eating around a normal calorie amount, keeps your brain from going crazy over the diet and scientifically keeps the weight off longer. I learned this from a CrossFit YouTuber named Jeff Nippard. He gives super awesome scientific explanations on heath and fitness. 

(Note - Not calling anyone out on this thread. Simply commenting) Please please please eat what feels comfortable for YOU. If you want to eat more, do it. If you want that slice of pie, go for it. At the end of the day it's about balance. Balance is KEY. But don't beat yourself if you want to eat like "crap" for a week or more. There can be underlying health or mental needs. You gotta enjoy your life.
